chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan narrated to me from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from Ahmad ibn Saffar, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Amr ibn Uthman, from one who narrated to him, from Harun ibn Harijah, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Do you establish all of your prayers in the Mosque of Kufah?' I said: 'No.' He said: 'If I were close to it, I would hope that no prayer would be missed by me in it.' He said: 'Do you know its merit?' I said: 'No.' He said: 'There is no righteous slave nor prophet except that he has prayed in the Mosque of Kufan.'

So much so that when the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) was taken on the Night Journey, Jibra'il (peace be upon him) said to him: 'Do you know where you are right now, O Muhammad?' He said: 'No.' He said: 'You are in front of the Mosque of Kufan.' So he said: 'Ask your Lord for permission so that I may descend and pray in it.' So he asked for permission and it was granted to him, so he descended and prayed two Rak'ah in it.
And indeed, the obligatory prayer in it equals one thousand prayers, and the recommended prayer in it equals five hundred prayers.

And indeed its front [its Qiblah] is a garden from the gardens of Paradise, and its right side is a garden from the gardens of Paradise, and its left side is a garden from the gardens of Paradise, and its back is a garden from the gardens of Paradise.
And indeed sitting in it without prayer or remembrance is worship, and if people knew what is in it, they would come to it even if they had to crawl.
ai.seo_question: What are the spiritual rewards and merits of praying in the Mosque of Kufah according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Kamil al-Ziyarat* underscores the cosmological significance of Kufah as a spiritual axis, linking terrestrial worship to the celestial realm through the Prophet’s Night Journey (Isra). It establishes a unique hierarchy of reward where the physical space itself becomes a locus of divine grace, with even passive presence yielding spiritual merit, reflecting the Shia emphasis on the sanctity of key geographical sites in Iraq.
